## TREELOCK1 — a session's tree is locked while the session holds it (2026-10-20, D51)

> - [ ] **TREELOCK1 — a session's tree is locked while the session holds it** (driver; D51, DOGFOOD1's first finding, the FIX-LOG's 2026-10-20 entry). A driven session's worktree is an unlocked git worktree on a branch at main's tip until its first commit, so any tool that prunes merged branches (a repository's own merge tool did, mid-session) takes it; the session then stops with no tree. Daoris locks the tree when it opens it (`git worktree lock --reason "daoris session <id>"`) and unlocks it when the session lets it go, before its own clean-up removes it. Proof: a tree test that the lock is held while the session runs and lifted at its end; `git worktree prune` and a remove without `--force` refuse it meanwhile.

**Outcome** 2026-10-20: a driven session's own tree is locked with `git worktree lock --reason "daoris session <id>"` from its record's open to its run's end (`SessionLocks`, held in `Driver.RunAsync` and `DriverContinuations.ContinueAsync`), kept while its record parks or goes on at the next look, and taken over by a later session in the same tree; the look's tidy lets go of a lock no running or waiting session holds before it tidies. A person's or an opening's lock is never touched; a conversation's tree is not locked. Proof `SessionLocksTests` and `SessionTreeLockTickTests`; the rule and what it rejected are D51's TREELOCK1 note.

## FABRIC-PIPELINE1 — a workflow routes its work into pipelines, and verification is a pipeline of its own (design) (2026-10-21, D192)

A repository's workflow begins at a start node that routes each piece of work into one of several pipelines the person configures; development and verification are kept apart: a development pipeline's sessions run only the light checks their change reaches (a heavy gate refused to them, as the heavy-run slot holds them today), and verification is its own CI-like pipeline that takes landed work, runs the declared heavy gates (`daoris.gates.json`) outside any session, batches what landed meanwhile, and turns a failure into work for the development pipeline. Written by Opus, read by Codex, the steward accepting (D191 and its note: Fable reads only if the design turns out to change a foundation). Proof: the design and its decision; then its build rows.

**Outcome** 2026-10-21: the design is written and accepted: `docs/2026-10-20-pipeline-design.md` and D192, after three rounds (Codex's read, 21 findings; Fable's of §2-§4, 29), every finding taken. A workflow's start is the choice table with a `landed` route resolved on its own; a pipeline is a named workflow its route chooses, a verification pipeline marked at its creation and landing nothing; a development pipeline's sessions run light checks only; verification is a never-skippable `check` Daoris performs off the pass through the performer's reconcile, each run to its verdict in a folder of its own, its declaration accepted by its blob id, its failures made fix asks. ## CODEXLOGIN1 — Codex signs in by the browser, as ChatGPT's desktop app does, where a workspace refuses device codes (2026-10-21, D125)

> - [ ] **CODEXLOGIN1 — Codex signs in by the browser, as ChatGPT's desktop app does, where a workspace refuses device codes** (driver, modules, web, CLI; the owner's report, 2026-10-21; D125's CODEXACCT2 note). Both doors sign in only by `codex login --device-auth` (`CodexAccounts`; the CLI's `codex` entry, `src/Daoris.Cli/src/agents/toolchain.ts:361`), and a ChatGPT workspace whose admin has not enabled device codes refuses it ("Please contact your workspace admin to enable device code authentication"), so that account cannot be added at all. CODEXACCT2 left the browser sign-in because its callback listens on port 1455, which a reserved Windows range covered that day; the ranges move on reboot, and 1455 was free on 2026-10-21. Wanted: a sign-in any account can complete. The browser sign-in (`codex login`: the system browser, then its local callback) is offered first where its port is free, and the device code beside it. Where the port is held, the panel says so and offers the other way, and the design decides whether Daoris's own browser takes the callback without the port. A refusal is read from the tool's line and said in the panel with the other way offered. The pinned version's flows are measured before they are declared (D57). Design first under D191, Codex's read. Proof: stand-ins for each case in `CodexAccountTests`, `DriverModuleSignInTests`, `toolchain.test.ts` and `SignIn.test.tsx` (the browser with its port free, the port held, the device code refused by the workspace), and the owner adding the account on the install.

**Outcome** 2026-10-21: built, on the steward's decisions in place of a design. Both doors run `codex login` first and `codex login --device-auth` beside it; the browser's ports (1455, else 1457, as 0.160.0 was measured to take them) are tried by binding before it starts, and where neither can be taken it is refused in plain words with the device code offered; a sign-in switches ways at any time, stopping the first; the panel and the terminal say the tool's refusal and offer the other way. Daoris's own browser taking the callback was found not possible within the toolchain contract, so no row was filed. Unproven until the install: the owner adding the workspace account. Detail: D125's CODEXLOGIN1 note.
